records.name: Kidney
verify: internal_structure: no BP3D concept exists for any internal kidney structure (cortex, medulla, pyramid, papilla, column, pelvis, calyx — 74-probe gap analysis in the inventory); the fields are sourced text on the two whole-kidney geometry records
records.note: The adrenal (suprarenal) glands sit immediately superior to the kidneys within a separate envelope of the renal fascia (S1). The source release files them under the endocrine system, not this module — see the inventory's adrenal_filing finding; they are endocrine module records, cross-referenced, never duplicated here. The renal vessels are cardiovascular module records, cited per field.
records.position: Bilateral bean-shaped organs, reddish-brown, in the posterior abdomen; they lie retroperitoneally either side of the vertebral column, typically extending from T12 to L3, the right kidney often slightly lower due to the presence of the liver; each kidney is approximately three vertebrae in length.
records.coverings: Deep to superficial: (1) renal capsule — a tough fibrous capsule; (2) perirenal fat — a collection of extraperitoneal fat; (3) renal fascia (Gerota's fascia) — encloses the kidneys and the suprarenal glands; (4) pararenal fat — mainly on the posterolateral aspect of the kidney.
records.internal_structure: The renal parenchyma divides into an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The cortex extends into the medulla (the renal columns), dividing it into triangular renal pyramids and separating the pyramids and renal papillae; the columns and pyramids together divide the kidney into 6-8 lobes. The apex of each pyramid is a renal papilla, and the papillae are bundles of collecting ducts that transport urine made by the nephrons to the calyces.
records.drainage_sequence: Renal papilla -> minor calyx (each papilla is associated with a minor calyx, which collects urine from the pyramid) -> major calyx (several minor calices merge) -> renal pelvis (the flattened, funnel-shaped expansion formed from the major and minor calyces within the hilum) -> ureter.
records.hilum: A deep fissure on the medial margin of each kidney, the gateway into the organ: normally the renal vessels and the ureter enter and exit via the hilum. The renal veins leave the hilum anteriorly to the renal arteries.
records.arterial_supply: Via the renal arteries (cardiovascular module records artery.renal-artery), arising directly from the abdominal aorta immediately distal to the origin of the superior mesenteric artery; the right renal artery is longer and crosses the inferior vena cava posteriorly. At the hilum the artery forms an anterior division (75% of supply) and a posterior division (25%), from which five segmental arteries originate; the segmental branches are end arteries with no communication between vessels. Intrarenal sequence: segmental -> interlobar (either side of every pyramid) -> arcuate -> interlobular -> afferent arteriole -> glomerulus -> efferent arteriole. Accessory renal arteries are common (in about 25% of patients).
records.venous_drainage: Via the left and right renal veins (cardiovascular module record vein.renal-vein), leaving the hilum anterior to the renal arteries and emptying directly into the inferior vena cava; the left renal vein is longer and travels anterior to the abdominal aorta below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
records.lymphatics: Lymph from the kidney drains into the lateral aortic (para-aortic) lymph nodes, located at the origin of the renal arteries.
records.relations: Anterior — left kidney: suprarenal gland, spleen, stomach, pancreas, left colic flexure, jejunum; right kidney: suprarenal gland, liver, duodenum, right colic flexure. Posterior — both: diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, transversus abdominis, and the subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves; the left kidney also the 11th and 12th ribs, the right kidney the 12th rib.

records.name: Nephron
verify: no BP3D concept: this structure has no concept in the BodyParts3D 4.0 release (see the inventory gap analysis); the record is sourced text without geometry — no nephron, glomerulus, capsule, tubule segment or collecting duct concept exists; the record links the two whole-kidney records it would subdivide

ta_name: not found in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — the string 'nephron' occurs in no TA2 term, synonym or related term in the consulted table; TA2 2.07 carries no nephron term.
records.note: The nephron is the load-bearing microscopic unit for the physiology follow-on: its segment order here is the sequence a renal compartment model must follow.
records.definition: The functional unit of the kidney: a renal corpuscle and a specialised tubule, with its own blood supply. Nephrons cleanse the blood of toxins and balance the constituents of the circulation to homeostatic set points through filtration, reabsorption and secretion; the filtrate they modify becomes urine.
segments_in_order: renal corpuscle (glomerulus within the glomerular capsule)
loop of Henle (descending and ascending limbs)
collecting duct (a common duct shared by many nephrons, draining to the renal papilla)
records.corpuscle: The glomerulus is a high-pressure capillary bed of fenestrated capillaries between the afferent and efferent arterioles. The glomerular (Bowman's) capsule surrounds it, captures the filtrate and directs it to the PCT; glomerulus and capsule together form the renal corpuscle.
records.types: All glomeruli lie in the cortex. Cortical nephrons have short loops of Henle that do not dip far beyond the cortex; about 15 percent of nephrons are juxtamedullary, with very long loops extending deep into the medulla. Blood exits the glomerulus into the efferent arteriole, which forms the peritubular capillary network around the tubule; for juxtamedullary nephrons the straight capillary portion following the loop deep into the medulla is the vasa recta.
records.juxtaglomerular_apparatus: Lying just outside the glomerular capsule: where the afferent and efferent arterioles enter and leave the capsule, the initial part of the DCT comes into direct contact with the arterioles, and the DCT wall there forms the macula densa, a part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA).

records.name: Ureter
verify: constrictions: no BP3D concept exists for any ureteric junction, part or orifice (probe-verified); the constrictions are sourced text on the two whole-ureter geometry records
records.extent: Two muscular tubes, one draining each kidney. Length as consulted: approximately 25 cm (S2); OpenStax gives approximately 30 cm (S4). The consulted sources differ, so the recorded extent is the range 25-30 cm.
records.course: Arises in the abdomen as a continuation of the renal pelvis; the point at which the pelvis narrows to form the ureter is the ureteropelvic junction. Abdominal part: descends on the anterior surface of the psoas major, retroperitoneal throughout. At the sacroiliac joints it crosses the pelvic brim (crossing the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries) and enters the pelvic cavity. Pelvic part: travels down the lateral pelvic walls; at the level of the ischial spines it turns anteromedially towards the bladder and pierces the bladder wall obliquely — a one-way valve (a physiological rather than anatomical sphincter) that prevents reflux of urine into the ureter. Urine is propelled by waves of peristalsis, not passive drainage.
constrictions: ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) — where the renal pelvis narrows to become the ureter
pelvic inlet — where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim
ureterovesical junction (UVJ) — where the ureter enters the bladder; the narrowest of the three
records.constriction_note: The three narrowings are the historically taught sites of ureteric calculus obstruction; more recent radiological and clinical evidence suggests stone impaction occurs predominantly at the upper ureter and the ureterovesical junction (S2).
records.arterial_supply: Abdominal part: renal artery, testicular/ovarian artery, and ureteral branches directly from the abdominal aorta. Pelvic part: superior and inferior vesical arteries. Venous drainage is by vessels corresponding to the arteries.
records.innervation: Via the renal, testicular/ovarian and hypogastric plexuses. Sensory fibres enter the spinal cord at T11-L2, with ureteric pain referred to those dermatomal areas.
records.relations_at_risk: Female: at the pelvic brim the ureter lies close to the ovaries (at risk in oophorectomy); about 2 cm superior to the ischial spine it runs underneath the uterine artery ('water under the bridge' — at risk in hysterectomy). Male: the vas deferens crosses the ureter anteriorly. The ureters must be identified during pelvic surgery to avoid accidental damage.

records.name: Urinary pathway
verify: sequence: the intrarenal stations (papilla, minor and major calyx, renal pelvis) have no BP3D concepts (probe-verified); the pathway is sourced text linking the six whole-organ geometry records
ta_name: not found in TA2 (FIPAT 2nd ed., version 2.07) consulted 2026-11-06 — project pathway construct (the urine pathway as a route, not a structure); TA2 names its organs individually.
records.function: Urine formed by the nephrons drains from the collecting ducts at the renal papillae into the minor calyces, which merge into the major calyces and the funnel-shaped renal pelvis in the hilum; the pelvis funnels urine by peristalsis into the ureter, which propels it to the bladder, where it is stored until micturition expels it through the urethra.

records.name: Urinary bladder
verify: parts: no BP3D concept exists for any bladder part or feature (apex, body, fundus, neck, trigone, detrusor — probe-verified); the fields are sourced text on the single whole-bladder geometry record

vasculature: no vesical artery or vein has a BP3D concept ('vesical artery'/'vesical vein' probes return zero hits) and the cardiovascular census carries no vesical record; the supply is sourced text (S3) only
records.position: A pelvic organ posterior to the pubic bone and anterior to the rectum; in females it lies anterior to the uterus, in males the prostate lies inferior to it. It is partially retroperitoneal: only its dome carries a peritoneal covering, which projects into the abdomen when the bladder is distended. When full it is oval; when empty it is flattened by the overlying bowel.
records.function: Two roles: temporary storage of urine — a hollow organ with distensible walls and a folded internal lining (rugae) — and assistance in the expulsion of urine, its musculature contracting during micturition with concomitant relaxation of the sphincters.
records.capacity: 400-600 mL in healthy adults (S3); OpenStax gives adult volumes ranging to 500-600 mL (S4).
parts: apex — located superiorly, pointing towards the pubic symphysis; connected to the umbilicus by the median umbilical ligament, a remnant of the urachus
body — the main part of the bladder, between the apex and the fundus
fundus (base) — located posteriorly, triangular-shaped with the tip of the triangle pointing backwards
neck — formed by the convergence of the fundus and the two inferolateral surfaces; continuous with the urethra
records.trigone: A triangular area within the fundus marked by the three orifices: the two ureteric orifices (urine enters from the ureters) and the internal urethral orifice (urine exits). Unlike the rest of the internal bladder, the trigone has smooth walls, explained by its different embryological origin — it develops by the integration of the two mesonephric ducts at the base of the bladder.
records.musculature: The bladder wall's specialised smooth muscle is the detrusor: irregular crisscrossing bands whose fibres run in all directions, retaining structural integrity when stretched and reducing the size of the organ when it empties. The interior surface is transitional epithelium, suited to the bladder's large volume fluctuations. Detrusor fibres often become hypertrophic (prominent trabeculae) when bladder emptying workload increases.
records.vasculature: Primarily derived from the internal iliac vessels. Arterial supply via the superior vesical branch of the internal iliac artery, supplemented in males by the inferior vesical artery and in females by the vaginal arteries (the obturator and inferior gluteal arteries may contribute small branches). Venous drainage by the vesical venous plexus into the internal iliac veins. Lymphatics: the superolateral aspect drains to the external iliac nodes; the neck and fundus drain to the internal iliac, sacral and common iliac nodes.
records.innervation: Sympathetic — hypogastric nerve (T12-L2): relaxes the detrusor, promoting urine retention. Parasympathetic — pelvic nerve (S2-S4): contracts the detrusor, stimulating micturition. Somatic — pudendal nerve (S2-S4): supplies the external urethral sphincter, giving voluntary control. Sensory nerves in the bladder wall report filling to the brain.

records.name: Urethra
verify: female: no BP3D concept — the release carries a single unsexed, undivided urethra (probes for 'male urethra', 'female urethra' and every named part return zero hits); the sexed anatomy is sourced text on the one urethra geometry record
male: no BP3D concept — as for female: no sexed form and no prostatic/membranous/spongy part exists in the release
records.note: The inventory's single urethra record is unsexed because the source release is; this record states the sex difference from the consulted sources and flags that neither sex's urethra has geometry of its own.
records.function: Transports urine from the bladder to the outside of the body for disposal. It is the only urologic organ that shows any significant anatomic difference between males and females; all other urine transport structures are identical. In the male it also transports semen.
records.female: Short — about 4 cm. The external urethral orifice is embedded in the anterior vaginal wall, inferior to the clitoris, superior to the vaginal opening (introitus) and medial to the labia minora. Its short length is less of a barrier to fecal bacteria than the longer male urethra — the best explanation for the greater incidence of urinary tract infection in women.
records.male: Averages 20 cm, in four regions in order: (1) preprostatic urethra — very short, incorporated into the bladder wall; (2) prostatic urethra — passes through the prostate gland immediately inferior to the bladder, receiving sperm via the ejaculatory ducts and secretions from the seminal vesicles; (3) membranous urethra — passes through the deep muscles of the perineum, invested by the urethral sphincters; (4) spongy (penile) urethra — passes through the corpus spongiosum and exits at the external urethral orifice at the tip of the penis.
records.sphincters: Internal urethral sphincter — smooth muscle under involuntary autonomic control at the bladder neck: in males, circular smooth fibres thought to prevent seminal regurgitation during ejaculation; in females, a functional sphincter formed by the anatomy of the bladder neck and proximal urethra (no sphincteric muscle present). External urethral sphincter — skeletal muscle under voluntary control, of the same structure in both sexes, innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4); in males its mechanism is more complex, correlating with fibres of the rectourethralis and levator ani.
records.epithelium: In both sexes the proximal urethra is lined by transitional epithelium and the terminal portion by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium; in the male, pseudostratified columnar epithelium lines the urethra between these two.
